name: Cesar Chavez
role: Labour leader and co-founder of the United Farm Workers (1927–1993)
summary: A farmworkers' union leader who co-founded the National Farm Workers Association and the United Farm Workers. He pursued change through nonviolent direct action such as boycotts, marches and fasts, grounded in Catholic social teaching and in Mexican-American and Chicano identity. He defended collective bargaining, attacked pesticide use and grower influence on politics, and changed his position on undocumented immigration over the 1970s.

automate-paid-work.rationale: His 1976 speech treats purposeful work as the cornerstone of human dignity, calls technology that turns people into robots crippling, and asks for more meaningful work for the unemployed, not less work.

civil-disobedience-accept-penalty.rationale: His record: in December 1970 he refused to obey a Salinas court injunction against the lettuce boycott and went to jail, held until he called it off, rather than comply or evade the sentence.

class-collaboration.rationale: Mixed: he said the union does not seek to destroy growers and would cooperate with employers who sign fair contracts, yet he treated strikes, boycotts and economic power as necessary against growers.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Says farm workers should be able to 'sit down and negotiate with your employer as equals across the bargaining table', and faults growers for refusing to bargain in good faith.

corporate-influence.rationale: Said agribusiness lobbying beats even the NRA, that lobbying kept farm workers out of federal safety laws, and that corporate growers gave Governor Deukmejian a million dollars and were repaid with a farm labor board that no longer enforced the law.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Describes his union as attacking the 'historical source of shame and infamy' imposed on Mexican-Americans and speaks of racism and discrimination as wrongs to be overcome.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: In 1968 he said Mexican-American leaders should fight like hell for welfare aid for those who truly need it, but in 1976 he called hand-outs to the unemployed stifling to the spirit and asked for meaningful work instead; he never proposed cutting welfare.

democracy-best.rationale: Describes the society he works within as 'a democratic society, where majority rules', and invokes the Bill of Rights in defending the union against charges of danger.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Recalled that the doctors, lawyers and professionals who joined CSO lacked the urgency of farm workers and liked to talk about playing politics; he was speaking of professionals in that organization, not university graduates generally.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Says farm workers 'are not agricultural implements' and insists his people be treated 'as human beings and not as chattel'.

family-wage.rationale: Said in the 1969 Senate statement that what he would like to see is a family living wage for every farm worker, and the 1984 address frames wages and conditions around supporting farm families.

farm-price-support.rationale: Asked Congress to consider the proposed National Agricultural Bargaining Act so producers could obtain fair prices in commodity markets and family farms a living income, though he criticized subsidies that mainly benefited large growers.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Counted overcoming discrimination in employment among the gains of union contracts and described discrimination as one of the evils the union exists to fight, which is the opposite of a right to refuse to hire on those grounds.

future-generations.rationale: Pleads for protection from poisons for 'our children and for their children', a concern for future generations that is not framed as stewardship of the Earth.

informal-organisation.rationale: His 1966 essay describes building a lasting dues-paying organization with a credit union and services for thousands of members, the strike being only a temporary condition, and he called the UFW first and foremost a union.

land-redistribution.rationale: Proposed that Congress study a national policy to enable farm workers to become family-sized farm owners and to reverse land concentration; he did not call for taking estates from their owners.

more-religion-public.rationale: In The Mexican-American and the Church (1968) he calls on the Church, as a powerful moral and economic force, to stand with farm workers and sacrifice with the people for social change, and says Mexican-Americans have a duty to appeal to it as naturally as to government.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Describes damage to the land as a 'wanton abuse of nature', which treats nature as worth protecting for its own sake, though he does not state this directly.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Listed water subsidies, farm subsidies and similar handouts to corporate growers as special privileges from an era of rural-dominated legislatures and said they could soon be in jeopardy, treating them as an unfair benefit to the well-connected.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Stresses farm workers 'seizing control over their own lives' through votes, union elections and voter registration drives.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: Calls the boycott 'a fight for the future of America' and speaks of 'one family', linking national interest with the welfare of workers.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Accused California’s governor of paying back donor growers at workers’ expense and called regulators captives of agribusiness; the criticism targeted politicians allied with growers, not all elites.

precautionary-principle.rationale: In the 1986 Wrath of Grapes speech he says no one can define safe exposure to residual poison, so consumers must be warned and act now.

priority-to-poor.rationale: In 1968 he wrote that the Church is called to be servant to the poor, that its wealth should be channeled to them, and that the state should provide welfare aid and education aid to all who need it.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Accuses growers of abusing and exploiting the workers who produce their wealth; he does not state a general theory of profit.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Objected to county agricultural commissioners refusing to disclose pesticide-application records and to court injunctions against disclosure, and in 1989 complained that farm workers are not told when pesticides are used; a narrow case of a general right.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Organised Mexican-American voters and workers as a community with shared interests, and Wikipedia reports he focused the movement on their ethnic identity.

racial-pride.rationale: Speaks of 'confidence and pride and hope' among Hispanics raised by the union, and of fighting for the dignity of his people.

reduce-immigration.rationale: His words point both ways: the 1974 Examiner letter backs amnesty and legal entry for Mexican workers, while in 1967 he told Congress that commuting green-card workers depress wages and break strikes and urged an investigation of that policy. The campaign against undocumented strikebreakers concerns unauthorized migration, not immigration levels, so it is left out.

religion-illusion.rationale: Frames his movement as a Christian one and speaks of God as the giver of life, so he does not regard religion as mere consolation.

resist-oppression-despite-death.rationale: In the 1969 Letter from Delano he says farm workers are in a death struggle against injustice, taught to resist with every ounce of endurance rather than flee, a struggle that ennobles their dying; his 1968 fast statement calls sacrificing ourselves for others in nonviolent struggle the truest courage.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Told the Senate that repressive legislation is not the answer to harvest strikes and boycotts, and asked for exemption from the Taft-Hartley and Landrum-Griffin bans on recognition picketing and secondary boycotts; in 1972 he condemned Arizona’s law barring farm boycotts.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Calls 'the greatest tragedy' a life without 'the satisfaction of giving life for others' and urges giving oneself totally to nonviolent struggle.

social-market-economy.rationale: Praised the New Deal (Social Security, unemployment insurance, Fair Labor Standards Act) as reforms within free enterprise and asked that farm workers get minimum wage and social insurance coverage.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Fast statements speak of 'spirits', God and a spiritual commitment to justice alongside the material struggle over wages and conditions.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: In his 1976 nominating speech he rejected the claim that technology alone can solve our problems, saying it too often means drudgery and turns people into robots.

unions-good.rationale: Calls the UFW 'first and foremost a union, a union like any other' and says it survives only by delivering bread-and-butter gains for members.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Asked Congress to study ways to reverse the concentration of farmland in fewer hands and to help farm workers become family-sized farm owners, said his natural sympathy lay with small growers, and in 1989 named mammoth agribusiness and huge farms as the problem.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Spent his life in political organising, voter registration and campaigns, and says the movement's power comes from struggle in public life.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Pressed for free, secret-ballot union elections among workers, but the record does not show a position on how companies themselves are run.

notes:
Positions were checked against his own words where available: the 1984 Commonwealth Club address (full transcript), the 1986 Wrath of Grapes excerpt, and his 1968 and 1972 fast statements. The Wrath of Grapes text is a seven-minute excerpt, not the full speech. The Foundation's archive and the 1968 nonviolence and 1975 farm labor law texts were unreachable, so the 1975 act is only covered through his 1984 speech. His immigration stance is the most contested part of the record. The 1974 letter (quoted via s5) is the most recent clear statement found on immigration, and the Illegals Campaign and wet line (both 1973–1974, reported in s4) point the other way, so the answer is 0 at low confidence. His Vietnam opposition and vegetarianism come from Wikipedia and are secondhand. No position was found on the great majority of statements, so most are null.

Merged with an independent claude-sonnet-5-5 audit: 18 answers taken from it, 22 agreed, 1 conflicts settled by the integrator.

claude-sonnet-5-5 notes: Historical figure; only positions he stated or acted on are recorded, and the two inferred answers are marked low. The 1966 essay (s1) covers only his organizing method. Immigration is left null: his 1969 Senate statement and 1974 Examiner letter oppose using undocumented workers as strikebreakers and favor legal residency (s4, s9), but a private 1974 letter and the 1974 Illegals Campaign (s11) show a harder line, and neither answers a statement about immigration levels. He supported the Vietnam Moratorium in 1969 but no statement matches. The 2026 allegations against him are not political positions and are not used.

claude-opus-5-5 deepening pass (2026-11-07, rules 5): read the maintainer-supplied text of The Organizer's Tale (same essay as b1) in full; searched the local hearings corpus (his 1967 House testimony on NLRA coverage, the 1969 S.8 hearing whose prepared statement is b4, INS hearing records of his 1973 telegram), and the web for his speeches (1976 nomination of Jerry Brown, Letter from Delano 1969, 1970 Salinas jailing, 1987 gay-rights march, Vietnam Moratorium, cooperatives, vegetarianism, health care). Themes searched: economy (welfare, health, minimum wage, cooperatives), society (religion, gay rights), liberty/government (civil disobedience, democracy), world (Vietnam, immigration), technology, means. Nulled three answers resting only on Wikipedia whose quotations could not be checked in the original. The UCSD Farmworker Movement archive (library.ucsd.edu) now refuses scripted access (bot check), as do ufw.org (403) and the UTA Mavmatrix copy of the Letter from Delano (Cloudflare check); his 1987 March on Washington speech for lesbian and gay rights and Levy's Autobiography of La Causa (archive.org, lending only) could not be read, so gay-rights and cooperative statements stay null. The Vietnam Moratorium support (1969) answers no statement. Most remaining nulls are things he never addressed.
